soil-phys-146.title: The hidden atmosphere between soil grains
soil-phys-146.text: After a long drought, the first rain releases a familiar scent. That smell is the soil's own atmosphere, flushed out of the ground as the rain soaks in. Soil gas is the mix of gases filling the air spaces between soil particles, the pores described in {{ref:soil-phys-069}}. Its main components are nitrogen, carbon dioxide and oxygen. Nitric oxide, nitrous oxide, methane and ammonia also occur naturally. Oxygen matters most to life below ground, because plant roots and soil organisms need it to respire. As they breathe, microbes and roots use up oxygen and release carbon dioxide. Soil air therefore holds less oxygen and more carbon dioxide than the air above. Gas and water share the same pore space. Gas moves in as water drains, evaporates or is taken up by roots, so the two are often inversely related. Soil air also carries messages. Soil organisms release volatile compounds as by-products of their metabolism, as chemicals that act on their neighbors and as signals. The result is a network of chemical cues. The soil's gas budget matters for climate too. Well-ventilated soil is a net sink of methane, yet oxygen-starved soil at higher temperatures produces it. Overall, soil is a net emitter of greenhouse gases, especially where {{ref:soil-env-129}} thaws and releases its gas as the climate warms.

soil-phys-137.title: How warm the ground runs, and why it matters
soil-phys-137.text: Across the world's biomes, mean annual soil temperature runs from −10 to 26 °C. Soil temperature is how warm or cold a soil is, set by the balance between the energy it absorbs and the energy it loses. It is one of the traits covered in {{ref:soil-phys-040}}, and a great deal of life depends on it. It regulates seed germination, the breaking of seed dormancy, plant and root growth and the availability of nutrients. Soil temperature varies by season, month and day, but the swings shrink with depth. Upper layers follow the air, while deeper layers fluctuate less. Water content, color, relief, plant cover and air temperature all shift it. Pale soils, which reflect more sunlight, stay cooler than dark ones. Water has a large effect. Wet surface soil is typically 3 to 6 °C colder than dry surface soil, because water takes more energy to heat and to evaporate. Covering the ground changes the picture as well. Clear plastic sheeting, or drying the soil, raises its temperature. A layer of plant material on the surface slows warming and damps surface swings. Farmers work around soil temperature. They time their planting, apply anhydrous ammonia below 10 °C (50 °F) and protect shallow-rooted crops from {{ref:soil-phys-153}}. Soil temperatures are now rising worldwide with climate warming. The main threats are the thaw of {{ref:soil-env-129}}, carbon loss and ecosystem collapse. How warming soils will affect carbon capture, storage and climate feedbacks is still disputed, and sources hold opposing views.

soil-phys-148.title: How oxygen finds its way into the ground
soil-phys-148.text: Soil air is never still. Its gas molecules move constantly, colliding and bouncing in a random walk. Gas diffusion is the net movement of those molecules through soil pores from higher to lower concentration. It is the main way {{ref:soil-phys-146}} trades with the atmosphere, and Fick's law describes it in numbers. Oxygen diffuses in from the air above and is consumed below. Excess carbon dioxide, other gases and water vapor diffuse out. The rate depends on total porosity, how well the pores connect, water content, air turbulence and temperature. Pore size itself matters less. Compaction lowers the diffusion coefficient, the measure of how readily gas spreads, and a platy structure also blocks the flow. Water is the great obstacle. In saturated soil no open air passages remain, and diffusion slows some 10,000 times. Short of oxygen, anaerobic bacteria, which live without free oxygen, reduce nitrate to N2, N2O and NO gases. This drains nitrogen from the soil. Daily and seasonal swings in temperature and moisture change the soil gas, and with it the pace of {{ref:soil-bio-033}}. When frozen soils thaw or dry soils are rewetted, microbes surge into activity. Sudden bursts of carbon dioxide and methane follow.

soil-phys-150.title: Letting the soil breathe
soil-phys-150.text: Compaction is one of the commonest reasons a soil runs short of air. Soil aeration is the exchange of gases between soil and atmosphere, along with the ways of improving it. Below ground, microbial activity and root respiration use up oxygen and build up carbon dioxide. A lack of oxygen can then hold back plant growth. Good aeration also lets water drain and roots grow. The pore network ventilates the soil, and wind, atmospheric pressure, convection and diffusion all drive the exchange. Soil structure strongly shapes the larger pores that control aeration, infiltration and drainage. Those pores fail in two common ways: water fills them, or compaction crushes them. Either way, nutrient uptake can fall, and bacteria short of free oxygen take it from nitrate instead. Remedies range from chemistry to animals. Liquid aeration applies solutions, commonly of ammonium lauryl sulfate, that break down dense particles and loosen compacted soil. Adding lime improves soil structure and so aeration. Digging megafauna, large burrowing animals, help too by disturbing the soil's layers.

soil-phys-147.title: Soil air: like the sky's, but rich in carbon dioxide
soil-phys-147.text: The air in soil pores can hold 10 to 100 times the atmosphere's 0.04% carbon dioxide. Soil air composition is the make-up of the soil atmosphere: similar to the air above, but richer in carbon dioxide and water vapor. One typical comparison gives soil air 79.2% nitrogen, 20.6% oxygen and 0.25% carbon dioxide, against 78.0%, 20.9% and 0.04% in the atmosphere. High carbon dioxide may inhibit root respiration, and at extreme levels it is toxic. It increases with depth, where dead plant material decomposes and roots are abundant. Soils rich in carbonates buffer it, while in acid soils the carbon dioxide that roots and microbes breathe out accumulates in the pores. Unlike the more uniform atmosphere, soil air shifts daily and seasonally. Temperature, atmospheric pressure, wind and rainfall all steer it. Methane and nitrous oxide are minor parts, but they matter for greenhouse gas flux and for human impacts on soils.

soil-phys-158.title: How deep the winter reaches
soil-phys-158.text: Across the contiguous United States, the deepest winter freezing ranges from 0 to 8 feet (2.4 m) below ground. The frost line, also called frost depth or freezing depth, is the depth to which groundwater in the soil is expected to freeze. It deepens toward the poles. It also depends on climate, on how well the soil and nearby materials transfer heat, and on nearby heat sources. Snow cover and asphalt insulate the ground, while homes warm it. During seasonal freezing and thawing, the shifting position of the frost line is called the frost front. In Arctic and Antarctic places freezing reaches year-round {{ref:soil-env-129}}, and a different term, {{ref:soil-env-147}}, is used instead. In the tropics the term can mean something else: the elevation below which frost does not occur. Building codes place foundations below frost depth, because {{ref:soil-phys-153}} can move them. Water and sewer pipes are buried below it too. Where shallow bedrock or utilities prevent deep trenches, pipes are insulated or warmed with heat tape instead.

soil-phys-153.title: Why frozen ground rises: Stephen Taber's answer
soil-phys-153.text: Water expands only about 9% when it freezes, too little to explain how far frozen ground can rise. Frost heaving is the upward swelling of soil in freezing weather as ice grows toward the surface from the freezing front. It needs three things. The soil's fine pores must pull water upward ({{ref:soil-phys-155}}). Water must be supplied from below, as by a water table. And freezing temperatures must reach into the soil. Water climbs to the freezing front by capillary action. There it feeds growing layers of ice, described in {{ref:soil-phys-154}}, that can lift soil 1 foot (0.30 m) or more. By 1930 Stephen Taber had shown the real cause: water migrates to the freeze line. He also found that benzene, which contracts as it freezes, heaves too. That ruled out volume change as the main mechanism. The damage is familiar. Uneven heave cracks road surfaces, helping form springtime potholes, and it damages building foundations. Even cold stores and ice rinks can freeze and lift the ground beneath them. Fill that does not heave, insulation or heating prevents it. At the very start of the freezing season, before the freezing front has gone deep, the same process appears as {{ref:soil-phys-159}}.

soil-phys-159.title: Needle ice, the frost that grows in columns
soil-phys-159.text: On a cold night, bare soil can sprout a crop of ice. Needle ice is a mass of needle-shaped ice columns that grow from groundwater at the soil surface. It forms when the soil is above 0 °C but the air at the surface is below 0 °C. Water rises by capillary action and freezes onto the growing column. It depends on ice segregation: supercooled water, chilled below freezing yet still liquid, freezes onto existing ice in a porous material. Soils high in silt and in {{ref:soil-bio-114}} suit it best. Needles are typically a few centimeters long. The recorded maximum is 10 cm, though specimens of 15–20 cm have been seen at Gerðuberg. Needle ice is frost heaving at its earliest, with no overlying soil to lift. The needles raise soil particles and crusts that settle unevenly when they melt. This disturbs streambanks, aids soil creep and helps shape {{ref:soil-phys-163}}. Heaved seedlings often die, because they do not resettle or their roots dry out. The ice has many names: frost pillars, Kammeis, shimobashira, and pipkrake, a Swedish term coined in 1907 by Henrik Hesselman.

soil-phys-140.title: The properties that steer heat through soil
soil-phys-140.text: Heat enters and leaves soil in three ways: radiation, conduction and convection. Soil thermal properties govern how that energy moves. They form a branch of soil physics used in engineering, climatology and agriculture. The two main ones measure how much heat a volume of soil stores, in J·m−3·K−1, and how well it passes heat along, in W·m−1·K−1. Each has its own entry later: {{ref:soil-phys-139}} and {{ref:soil-phys-141}}. Together they decide how energy is shared out through the soil profile. Basic composition matters, but water content and the volume fractions of solids and air matter strongly. Moisture and thermal properties are so closely linked that they are often measured and reported together. Both change constantly with daily and seasonal cycles, which makes general statements about any one site hard. Surface temperature swings reach deeper layers more slowly and with a delay, an effect explored in {{ref:soil-phys-142}}. The uses are broad. Engineers weigh frost effects on construction and on buried pipes and cables, and farmers time their planting. Others study greenhouse gases, store radioactive waste or search for buried land mines.

soil-env-129.title: Permafrost, ground frozen for ages
soil-env-129.text: The oldest permafrost has stayed frozen for around 700,000 years. Permafrost is soil, rock or underwater sediment that stays continuously below 0 °C for two years or more. In practice it occurs where the mean annual temperature is 0 °C or below. It underlies about 11% of the global land surface, around 18 million km2. That includes much of Alaska, Canada, Greenland and Siberia, and high mountains such as the Tibetan Plateau. Its thickness ranges from less than a meter to more than 1,500 m. On land it usually lies beneath soil that freezes and thaws with the seasons, the {{ref:soil-env-146}}. Over millennia, dead plant and animal remains have built up in it without fully breaking down. That makes tundra soil a store of carbon. Warming now threatens that store. As permafrost thaws, the remains begin to break down again, releasing carbon dioxide or methane, which feeds back into climate change. Thaw also weakens the ground itself. Ice-rich soil can suddenly exceed hydraulic saturation and shift or collapse, endangering the buildings and infrastructure on it.

soil-phys-154.title: Ice lenses, the hidden engine of frost heave
soil-phys-154.text: Most of the lift in frost heave comes from ice growing in hidden layers underground. An ice lens is a body of ice that forms where moisture moving through soil or rock collects in one zone, usually parallel to the surface. Ice first gathers in small pores or cracks. It keeps collecting there, wedging the soil or rock apart. Lenses grow several centimeters to several decimeters deep, and their growth is the dominant cause of soil displacement in frost heaving. They draw water from groundwater below the freezing line, through fine soils with capillary pores. The water can travel because water in fine pores stays liquid below the normal freezing point, the Gibbs–Thomson effect. The same ice segregation splits rock more effectively than the freeze-thaw expansion proposed by older texts. Arctic tundra favors deep lenses, because permafrost keeps the ground frozen at depth and stops meltwater draining away.

soil-phys-149.title: Reading soil gas for oil and earthquakes
soil-phys-149.text: Gas seeping from the ground can hint at oil beneath it. Soil gas surveys put soil gases to work in research. Microseepage, the small release of hydrocarbons at the surface, is used to search for petroleum, on the assumption that hydrocarbons migrate vertically. The migration of soil gases, especially radon, is studied as a possible warning of earthquakes. Landfill waste, mining and petroleum contamination also produce gases, including volatile organic compounds, that diffuse through soil. Exchange between soil gas and the air can be analyzed by distance from the soil surface.

soil-phys-157.title: Mounds, pingos and polygons raised by frost
soil-phys-157.text: Frost heaving builds whole landscapes of mounds, on Earth and on Mars. Frost-heave landforms are raised-ground features arranged in circles, polygons and stripes. In organic soils such as {{ref:soil-class-070}} they are called palsas; in mineral soils, {{ref:soil-phys-161}}. They appear in alpine regions even near the equator, as palsas on Mount Kenya show. Pingos grow up to 60 meters high over hundreds of years in Arctic permafrost, fed by upwelling groundwater rather than capillary action. Small earth hummocks in seasonally frozen ground go by thúfur in Iceland and pounus in Fennoscandia. In May 2008 the Phoenix lander touched down on polygonal frost-heave ground on Mars and found ice a few centimeters down.

soil-phys-155.title: Which soils heave, and which do not
soil-phys-155.text: Frost-susceptible soil has pore sizes and particle surface area that promote capillary flow, so it can feed ice lenses and heave when it freezes. Silty and loamy soils, which contain fine particles, are the typical examples. Many agencies call a material frost susceptible if 10 percent or more passes a 0.075 mm (No. 200) sieve. Passing 3 percent or more through a 0.02 mm (No. 635) sieve also counts. Dense clays pass water too slowly. Clean sands and gravels have pores too open for capillary flow. For pavements, standard tests compare a soil's heave rate and thawed bearing ratio with an established classification.

soil-phys-156.title: How soil grains travel through solid ice
soil-phys-156.text: A grain of soil can move through solid ice. The key is premelting: thin films of liquid water persist on ice below freezing. Faraday reported this unfrozen layer in 1860 and called the particle migration thermal regelation. The film is thinner on a particle's cold side. Water keeps flowing from the warm side to the cold side and refreezing, so the particle moves toward warmer soil. A 10-nanometer film around a micrometer-sized particle can move it 10 micrometers a day, in a thermal gradient as low as 1 °C m−1. The process purifies growing ice lenses by pushing fine particles away.

soil-phys-163.title: Patterned ground: circles and stripes drawn by frost
soil-phys-163.text: Stones sorted into neat circles and stripes can form with no human hand involved. Patterned ground is the distinct, often symmetrical geometric patterns formed when ground material deforms in periglacial regions, cold lands shaped by frost. It occurs wherever soil freezing and thawing alternate, from the Arctic and Antarctica to the Australian Outback, the Atacama Desert and Mars. Computer models of the past 20 years tie its formation to frost heaving of wet, fine-grained, porous soils. Repeated freezing and thawing push larger stones up. Sideways forces pile them into clusters and stripes that smooth into polygons, circles and stripes. Circles range from a few centimeters to several meters across, and stripes form on slopes of 2° to 7°. Steps occur too, and each form is either sorted or unsorted. Polygons form either in permafrost, as ice wedges, or in areas of seasonal frost. Most of it forms in the seasonally thawing layer above permafrost, where the churning described in {{ref:soil-form-034}} also works.

soil-phys-161.title: Lithalsas, stony mounds lifted by ice
soil-phys-161.text: On the Svalbard archipelago, stony mounds have been heaved up out of the ground. They are lithalsas: frost-raised mounds in permafrost areas with mineral-rich soils, where a perennial ice lens, one that lasts year after year, has grown within the soil. A lithalsa is the mineral-soil counterpart of the palsa among the frost-heave landforms. The term is sometimes also used for palsas and pingos.

soil-phys-151.title: Spikes and cores: punching air into turf
soil-phys-151.text: Some lawn aerators are nothing more than spiked shoes. Core and spike aeration improves gas exchange mechanically. It either punctures the soil with spikes or removes cores about 1 in × 2 in (25 mm × 51 mm). Spike aerators use spikes up to a foot or more long and are sometimes used for drainage problems in turf. Core aeration on turf reduces compaction and {{ref:soil-bio-084}}, lets water and nutrients infiltrate better and encourages deeper roots. Machines range from walk-behind and ride-on models to tractor-pulled rigs.

soil-phys-139.title: Why wet soil is slow to warm
soil-phys-139.text: A gram of pure water needs about 1 calorie to warm by 1 °C; a gram of dry soil needs about 0.2. That quantity, the energy needed to raise a material's temperature by 1 °C, is its specific heat. For soil it is called soil heat capacity. Wet soil lies between 0.2 and 1, or 0.8 to 4.2 kJ per kilogram, and its specific heat rises with water content. Evaporating water also absorbs about 584 cal/g (2442 kJ/kg at 25 °C). So wet soil warms more slowly than dry soil. Volumetric heat capacity, in J·m−3·K−1, is one of the main soil thermal properties.

soil-phys-160.title: Frost boils, mud circles that churn for centuries
soil-phys-160.text: In Svalbard, the centers of frost boils heaved about 9.5 mm per day, against about 1.6 mm per day at their margins. A frost boil, or mud circle, is a small circular mound of fresh soil. Frost action and the churning in {{ref:soil-form-034}} form it. Typically 1 to 3 meters across, frost boils occur in periglacial or alpine areas with permafrost. They are among the commonest features of patterned ground. Each is a nonsorted circle: a barren mineral-soil center among vegetated, peaty ground. The wetter silty or loamy centers grow more ice lenses and heave more than their surroundings. Over years, soil is carried upward, in a cycle that can take centuries.

soil-phys-152.title: Linear aeration: grooves that feed the soil
soil-phys-152.text: One pass of a machine can spread organic amendments, cut grooves and close them again. That is linear aeration, which cuts grooves into soil or turf so that water and amendments penetrate and are retained in the right amounts. Because the grooves close in the same pass, soil structure is barely disturbed. The method can add {{ref:soil-bio-089}}, topsoil, {{ref:soil-fert-028}}, sand or clay as soil softeners where needed. On lawns it relieves excess water and compaction in heavily used areas, with less surface disruption than coring.

soil-phys-144.title: Seeing soil heat from the sky
soil-phys-144.text: Reflected light reveals only the topmost few molecular layers of a soil. Thermal remote sensing of soil looks deeper. Thermal infrared sensors on satellites and aircraft detect variations in soil thermal properties at shallow depths below the surface. They pick up heat moving into and out of near-surface layers by conduction, convection and radiation. Satellite microwave sensing helps too. Unlike thermal infrared, it is not affected by cloud cover.

soil-phys-141.title: Quartz, water and air: how well soil conducts heat
soil-phys-141.text: Quartz conducts heat at 8.8 W·m−1·K−1; dry soil manages only 0.2–0.4. Soil thermal conductivity is the ability of soil to conduct heat. In the same units, typical values are 0.57 for water, 0.25 for {{ref:soil-bio-114}} and 1–3 for wet soil. Air conducts heat poorly and weakens conduction through the solid and liquid parts. The solid phase conducts best, yet the varying moisture of a soil largely decides its conductivity. Designing a shallow-loop ground source heat pump needs an accurate on-site reading, which a thermal heat probe can provide.

soil-phys-138.title: Measuring the flow of heat into the ground
soil-phys-138.text: When the surface is warmer than the soil below, heat is conducted down into the soil. Soil heat flux is the rate at which heat moves through soil in response to a temperature difference between two points. Its density, in W·m−2, is the energy flowing through a unit area per unit time, with both a size and a direction. It is calculated from Fourier's law, using the soil's thermal conductivity and the temperature gradient between two depths. Heat flows against that gradient, from the warmer point to the cooler one.

soil-phys-164.title: Thermal diffusivity: how fast heat spreads
soil-phys-164.text: Air at 300 K has a thermal diffusivity of 19 mm2/s; water at 25 °C has just 0.143. Thermal diffusivity measures how fast heat spreads through a material, in m2/s. It equals thermal conductivity divided by density and specific heat capacity: α = k/(ρcp). The product ρcp is the volumetric heat capacity, in J/(m3·K). A material of high diffusivity conducts heat quickly relative to how much energy it stores, so heat moves through it rapidly. Sandstone sits at 1.15 mm2/s and ice at 0 °C at 1.02. In the field, the dual-probe heat-pulse sensor measures diffusivity together with volumetric heat capacity.

soil-phys-143.title: Needle probes that read soil heat in place
soil-phys-143.text: Two needles in the ground can yield all of a soil's main thermal properties. The heat probe method measures soil thermal properties in place, with needle probes that heat the soil and record its temperature response. A single probe heats continuously and senses how fast heat is conducted away, so it measures thermal conductivity only. IEEE 442-1981 and ASTM D 5334-08 cover it. The dual-probe heat-pulse method sets a heater and a sensor needle a fixed distance apart and records the sensor's response to a heat pulse over time. It measures thermal diffusivity and volumetric heat capacity, and conductivity follows from them. Its drawbacks are a small measured volume and sensitivity to probe-to-soil contact and heater-to-sensor spacing.

soil-phys-142.title: Thermal lag: deep soil warms late and gently
soil-phys-142.text: About 50% of the Sun's heat is absorbed at the surface, where temperature swings with day and night, weather and season. Thermal lag is this damping and delay with depth: deeper soil reaches its highs and lows later and less sharply. As a result the ground below the surface is warmer than the air in winter and cooler in summer. Deep enough down, temperature stays constant year round, at about the mean of summer and winter temperatures. Sources differ on that depth. Reported values include 5–6 m, 6 m and 15 m, and 4.25 m for dry soil against 6.7 m for wet soil.

soil-phys-145.title: Banking summer sun in the ground for winter
soil-phys-145.text: The ground can carry summer's solar energy into winter. Ground heat storage uses the earth as a long-term store of heat for ground source heat pumps. The thermal effusivity of soil, its ability to exchange heat with its surroundings, lets the ground serve as underground thermal energy storage. Design criteria for shallow-loop heat pumps require an accurate on-site reading of thermal conductivity. Earth-sheltered buildings draw on the same effect. The thermal mass and thermal lag of the surrounding earth keep their need for extra heating and cooling minimal.

openers.soil-temperature-and-air: Between the grains of every soil lies a second atmosphere. Soil gas fills the air spaces between particles, much like the air above but richer in carbon dioxide and water vapor, and it trades with the open air mainly as molecules drift through the pores from higher to lower concentration. Soil also has a temperature, set by the balance between the energy it absorbs and the energy it loses, and heat moves through it by radiation, conduction and convection. This chapter follows both, from the air that roots breathe to the depth where groundwater freezes. It ends in the cold: ice that swells the ground upward, needle-shaped columns that rise on frosty nights, and ground that stays below 0 °C for two years or more.

reviews.soil-temperature-and-air: Water ties this chapter together, because it competes with air for the same pores and slows the soil's warming. Roots and microbes use up oxygen and release carbon dioxide, so soil air depends on diffusion, which slows some 10,000 times once water fills the pores. Wet soil also stores more heat and conducts it better than dry soil, while temperature swings at the surface fade and lag with depth. When freezing reaches below the surface, water drawn up through silty soils feeds ice lenses that heave roads, uproot seedlings and sort stones into patterned ground. Where the ground stays frozen as permafrost, thaw threatens to release carbon dioxide and methane from dead remains stored there for millennia.
